/SUNDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 103 AM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Sunday and Monday: For the start of November, an active couple of 
days is anticipated, with high impact flooding expected across the 
already soaked southwestern mountains. A dynamic storm pattern will 
take shape, with the sub-tropical jet pushing northward, and a 
digging trough interacting with this. Confidence at this point is 
very high (>80%) in this upcoming pattern. As these two large scale 
features interact, another round of prolonged and heavy 
precipitation is anticipated across our mountains, with the heaviest 
falling across the San Juan Mountains. On the front side of this 
storm system, the airmass will be relatively warm, leading to higher 
snow levels Sunday, around 11,000-12,000+ft, and rain for a majority 
of the region. Then on the backside of the system, cooler Pacific 
air will filter in and drop snow levels to around 9,000-10,000ft by 
Monday morning. Overall, the warm and moist nature of this storm 
system is what will cause issues. This will favor a significant 
amount of precipitation falling as rain, with QPF totals ranging 
from 2-4 inches. This amount of liquid on top of already highly 
saturated soils, water laden snow, and running into rivers that are 
already elevated from last weeks rain event, will likely lead to 
another highly impactful flood event across the southwestern 
mountains and into the San Luis Valley. Currently, local rivers in 
that region are forecasted to quickly rise into Moderate to Major 
flood stages heading through Monday, with some rivers nearing record 
crest levels. Folks, the window for flood preparations is closing. 
Preparations should be ongoing and finished by this afternoon. Do 
not wait until it starts to rain and do not wait until the waters 
start to rise... by then it is too late. Then as alluded to, snow 
levels will start to lower heading through Sunday night and into 
Monday morning, which will transition some of the rain into snow, 
with around 12-15 inches of heavy, wet snow anticipated with this 
entire storm system. This will likely cause travel impacts along the 
southwestern mountain roadways, with dangerous and slick road 
conditions, especially Sunday night into Monday morning. Across the 
rest of the higher terrain, additional heavy, wet snow can be 
expected, though to a lesser degree, with ranges typically from 4-10 
inches. Elsewhere for the valleys and plains, rain scattered to 
numerous showers can be expected through this period. The greatest 
coverage for the valleys will be Sunday, with the greatest coverage 
then shifting eastward across the plains Monday as the storm system 
pushes east and a cold front drops southward. Along with all of 
that, strong winds can be expected both days, with gusty 
southwesterly winds Sunday on the front side of the storm system, 
with gusts of 30-50 mph, especially for the mountains, San Luis 
Valley, and eastern plains. Then gusty winds can be expected again 
Monday, as northwesterly winds develop on the backside of the storm 
system, with gusts again 30-50 mph, especially across the eastern 
plains. There is potential for winds to be stronger across the 
plains Monday night into Tuesday morning, but confidence on that is 
low (30%) at this time, at it will be highly dependent on how the 
trough evolves Monday night. Finally, to round things out for this 
stretch, mostly cloudy to cloudy skies can be anticipated with the 
stormy pattern in place, with temperatures warm and above seasonal 
values Sunday, and then cooling some Monday as the system passes and 
the aforementioned cold front starts dropping southward.

Tuesday - Friday: For the remainder of the long term period, periods 
of active weather are likely for portions of south central and 
southeastern Colorado. Overall, an active pattern will continue, 
with the Sunday - Monday storm system exiting Tuesday and additional 
waves within the flow passing over the region after that. Tuesday's 
exiting system will bring gusty winds early in the day, especially 
across the plains, with the later week features bringing increased 
precipitation chances, particularly for the mountains. While 
uncertainty does exist in how some of these waves will ultimately 
evolve, confidence is high (60-70%) about the unsettled pattern. 
Otherwise, breezy winds and uptick in cloud cover can be anticipated 
with these wave passages. As for temperatures, a fairly steady trend 
of mild temperatures can be expected.
